question: According to Graham Weaver, how should someone approach a difficult life change instead of staying on autopilot?

S1.title: How to break out of autopilot and create the life you want | Graham Weaver (Stanford GSB professor)
S1.text:

So if you realize this and instead ask the question, the version of myself five years from now, what would they wish I was going to do right now? So I can guarantee your five-year version of yourself will say, "Get out of that toxic relationship, no matter how painful it is for the next two months." And if you can make decisions from that, and then on top of that, realize it's going to get worse first, then that's why I say everything you want is on the other side of worse first. But if you don't do that, you just end up plateauing. And so many people I see have this happen where they hit a plateau and they never move past it because they're not willing to have that hard day, month, week, year whatever it is.

answer.summary: Get intentional about the life you want, ask what your future self would want you to do now, and take the step even though it may feel frightening and get harder before it gets better.

sections.heading: Choose deliberately, not on autopilot
sections.content: Make space to ask where you want your life to go, what matters to you, and what you would wish you had started ten years from now. Then work backward from that direction; Weaver also recommends making your calendar reflect your intentions.

sections.heading: Use your future self as a guide
sections.content: For a hard decision, ask what the version of yourself five years from now would wish you would do right now. Weaver illustrates this with leaving a toxic relationship despite the pain expected over the next two months.

sections.heading: Expect discomfort and act without waiting for perfect timing
sections.content: A change may feel worse at first: even starting at the gym can be unpleasant, and difficult changes can involve a hard day, month, week, or year. Weaver cautions that waiting until you feel secure, ready, or certain the timing is right can become “not ever”; some reasons to delay are legitimate, but others are fear in another form.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately attributes to Weaver the advice to ask what your five-years-from-now self would want you to do, expect a change to feel worse or uncomfortable at first, and act despite that short-term difficulty. Its additional points about intentionality and not waiting for perfect timing are supported by the cited context.
